::: {.kw-overview}
Xenotransplantation dominates this issue, and for once with clinical rather than preclinical data: the first report of a gene-edited porcine kidney supporting a living recipient for the best part of a year and then being explanted without leaving the patient sensitised against a subsequent human allograft, paired with a mechanistic review arguing that the proteinuria which has bedevilled pig-to-primate models may arise from several overlapping injury pathways at once. Rejection and its measurement supply the second thread. An open-label extension of the felzartamab phase 2 trial makes the case that late antibody-mediated rejection behaves as a chronic effector process needing sustained CD38 blockade rather than a finite course, and uses donor-derived cell-free DNA to time re-dosing, while a four-centre prospective validation study delivers a clean negative verdict on FDG-PET as a non-invasive way of avoiding the three-month surveillance biopsy. Two papers refine how we counsel and monitor: a meta-analysis finds no association between crescents in the native IgA nephropathy biopsy and recurrence in the allograft, and another pooling more than four thousand recipients shows the combined creatinine–cystatin C equation is the least biased way of estimating graft function, with the two single-marker equations erring in opposite directions and thus affecting long-term graft survival estimates. The issue closes on cardiometabolic risk, with a small matched cohort of dapagliflozin in diabetic recipients, and on living donation, where an Australian and New Zealand registry analysis shows nearly six-fold variation in living donor transplant rates between referral networks.
:::

---

### 1. [Porcine kidney xenotransplantation as a bridge to allotransplantation: a first-in-human study](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(26)01295-X)
[Riella LV, Borges TJ, Rosales IA, Avillach CT, Palsson R, Hullekes F, Verhoeff R, Pomahac A, Chen JY, Santagata S, Giarraputo A, Smith RN, Le HN, Barth JA, Low SC, Getchell K, Curtis M, Perrin S, Kolev M, Bercovici S, Lindner MS, Ribas GT, Tanguturi VK, Bapat AC, Pattanayak V, Longchamp A, El-Khoury J, Duggan M, Shah S, Pierson R, Madsen JC, Fishman JA, Elias N, Colvin RB, Kawai T. *Lancet*, 2026. PMID: 42692038.]{.kw-ref}

The three questions that have hung over clinical kidney xenotransplantation — how long a xenograft lasts, whether it transmits porcine pathogens, and whether it sensitises the recipient against future human organs — are all addressed by this single-patient report, the first of a planned three-patient study run under a US Food and Drug Administration Expanded Access Investigational New Drug application. The recipient had end-stage kidney disease, a long anticipated wait for a deceased donor organ and no suitable living donor, and received at Massachusetts General Hospital a gene-edited porcine kidney (EGEN-2784, eGenesis) in which the major glycan xenoantigens had been deleted, porcine endogenous retroviruses inactivated and seven human transgenes inserted, under costimulation blockade-based immunosuppression with complement inhibition. The graft worked immediately from the day of transplantation on 25 January 2025 and kept the patient off dialysis for 271 days. A day-14 biopsy showed T-cell-mediated rejection that resolved with treatment, and function then held for roughly six months until immunosuppression was cut back because of a bacterial — not zoonotic — infection, after which microvascular inflammation with endothelial injury appeared and progressed to thrombotic microangiopathy, ending in graft failure and nephrectomy. What makes that failure interesting is that the donor-specific crossmatch stayed persistently negative and the infiltrate on tissue analysis was dominated by macrophages and natural killer cells with minimal T-cell involvement, which the authors read as evidence that mechanisms beyond conventional antibody-mediated rejection drove the late injury. Surveillance including metagenomic sequencing detected no porcine pathogen transmission, and anti-HLA antibodies were unchanged throughout. Eighty-two days after the xenograft was removed the patient received a human kidney allotransplant, which functioned immediately with no evidence of sensitisation across 231 days of follow-up. The authors are careful to frame this as showing that xenotransplantation can provide prolonged dialysis-free support and be stopped without clinically significant allosensitisation, rather than as a demonstration of durability. For a UK unit this is not yet a clinical option — but the bridge concept it establishes, keeping a highly disadvantaged waiting-list patient off dialysis without spending their allosensitisation budget, is the framing in which xenotransplantation is most likely to reach a British transplant meeting, and the single-patient design means every one of these observations needs replication in the two remaining recipients before any of it can be generalised.

### 2. [PROTEINURIA AFTER PIG KIDNEY XENOTRANSPLANTATION: A POTENTIAL UNIFYING HYPOTHESIS LINKING MECHANICAL, INNATE, AND ADAPTIVE INJURY PATHWAYS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.08.015)
[Tripathi S, Terashita M, Rosales I, Cooper DKC. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42680012.]{.kw-ref}

Where the Lancet report describes what happened in one patient, this review tackles the complication that has most consistently limited pig-to-nonhuman-primate kidney xenografts and asks whether it will follow the field into the clinic. The authors are explicit that severe proteinuria has not so far emerged as a consistent finding in published human renal xenotransplant reports, and they treat its relevance in living human recipients as an unresolved question rather than an established problem. In the primate models the stakes are higher than protein loss alone: heavy proteinuria may be accompanied by urinary loss of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies, anti-CD154 among them, which would undermine the very rejection prophylaxis the model depends on. The lesions they associate with proteinuria in this setting are heterogeneous and overlapping, spanning immune and non-immune injury and including thrombotic microangiopathy, capillaritis, C4d deposition and xenograft glomerulopathy — a list that maps closely onto the microvascular injury pattern seen in the Lancet case. Haemodynamic mismatch between a porcine kidney and a primate or human circulation, often invoked as the driver, is downgraded here to a possible but unproven contributor rather than the dominant initiating trigger. What the authors offer instead is a deliberately provisional unifying hypothesis, presented as an evidence-informed and testable framework rather than a settled causal cascade, intended to prompt debate. Their practical recommendations are for correlating proteinuria with biopsy findings in individual cases and prospectively monitoring urinary drug loss, so that preventive strategies can be built on identified mechanisms. Read alongside the first-in-human report, it is a useful reminder for anyone assessing xenotransplantation data that the injury patterns being reported are not yet mechanistically understood, and that a negative crossmatch does not mean the graft is not being attacked.

### 3. [Prolonged CD38 targeting with felzartamab in antibody-mediated kidney transplant rejection: a biomarker-guided open-label phase 2 extension](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanepe.2026.101768)
[Mayer KA, Diebold M, Schrezenmeier EV, Halloran PF, Haindl S, Schatzl M, Akifova A, Allmer DM, Schranz S, Kozakowski N, Kläger J, Amann K, Beck J, Schütz E, Naesens M, Loupy A, Raynaud M, Görzer I, Vietzen H, Ingle G, Flesher DL, Patel UD, Halleck F, Graf I, Jilma B, Budde K, Böhmig GA. *Lancet Reg Health Eur*, 2026. PMID: 42471965.]{.kw-ref}

The felzartamab phase 2 trial showed that CD38 blockade could reduce antibody-mediated rejection activity but that the disease came back once treatment stopped, and this open-label extension asks whether continuing the drug — and using a biomarker to decide when — holds the response. Of the 21 patients who completed the randomised trial at Vienna and Charité Berlin, eleven with persistent or recurrent rejection entered a further 12 months of felzartamab at 16 mg/kg intravenously: six months of fixed dosing on the original nine-infusion schedule, then six months in which re-dosing was triggered by monthly donor-derived cell-free DNA exceeding 0.5% relative, 50 copies/mL absolute, or a doubling from the week-24 value. Median age at entry was 54 years and median eGFR 39 mL/min/1.73 m²; Banff phenotypes were chronic active rejection in six, active in three and probable in two. Median microvascular inflammation fell from 2 (IQR 2–2) at baseline to 1 (0–2) at week 24 and 0 (0–2) at week 52 (p = 0.011), with 7 of 11 (64%) scoring zero at the end, and the molecular rejection probability dropped from 0.77 (0.58–0.87) to 0.14 (0.06–0.29) at week 24 and 0.12 (0.08–0.35) at week 52 (p = 0.001). Donor-derived cell-free DNA fell from a baseline median of 45 copies/mL and 1.12% to 15 copies/mL and 0.25% at week 52, and during the guided phase levels dropped from 37.5 to 9.5 copies/mL a month after each triggered infusion, on a median of only two doses over six months at a median 12-week interval. Function was stable, with a median eGFR slope of +1.99 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI −0.64 to +4.63) against the −4 to −8 typically seen in late antibody-mediated rejection, and iBox-predicted seven-year death-censored graft survival rose from 63.5% to 80.8%. The response was not uniform: five patients still had active or chronic active rejection at week 52, three of them with cell-free DNA below threshold, natural killer cell counts failed to fall or re-expanded in some non-responders despite three or more doses, and immunodominant donor-specific antibody levels barely moved throughout — reinforcing the trial's central idea that effector mechanisms rather than antibody titre drive the tissue injury. Tolerability was acceptable, with 101 adverse events over 12 months, nine patients experiencing infusion reactions (which recurred after treatment-free intervals of three months or more), seven with serious adverse events none judged drug-related, and no discontinuations. The authors are appropriately restrained about the uncontrolled design, the small and selected "transplant survivor" cohort and the exploratory, reactive nature of a cell-free-DNA trigger that only fires once injury is underway; for UK units the practical read is that this is the strongest signal yet that late rejection needs continuous rather than finite immunomodulation, but the phase 3 trial and its fixed-dose comparison must report before any of this changes a treatment protocol.

### 4. [A multicenter prospective validation cohort does not support the use of kidney/psoas [18F]FDG uptake in the diagnosis of kidney allograft subclinical rejection](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345426)
[Lovinfosse P, Bouquegneau A, Massart A, Pipeleers L, Bonvoisin C, Carp L, Everaert H, Jadoul A, Dendooven A, Geers C, Grosch S, Erpicum P, Hellemans R, Seidel L, Weekers L, Hustinx R, Jouret F. *PLoS One*, 2026. PMID: 42685129.]{.kw-ref}

Surveillance biopsy remains the only way to detect rejection in a patient whose graft function looks perfectly stable, and FDG-PET has been proposed as the non-invasive test that could spare most of those biopsies — a proposition this Belgian multicentre study set out to validate prospectively and did not. Between January 2021 and March 2025 the investigators paired a protocol biopsy with FDG-PET/CT at roughly three months post-transplant in adult recipients across four independent imaging centres, expressing cortical uptake as a ratio of mean standardised uptake value in kidney cortex to that in psoas muscle. Of 185 patients, Banff 2022 classification gave 158 normal, 18 borderline and 9 with subclinical rejection (6 T-cell-mediated, 3 microvascular inflammation) — a low event rate that is itself part of the story. Uptake ratios were closely overlapping across the three histological groups at 2.33 (1.97–2.93) in normal, 2.71 (2.50–3.33) in borderline and 2.42 (2.27–3.14) in subclinical rejection, and there was no correlation between the ratio and the total inflammation score (R = 0.032, p = 0.67). In centre-stratified multivariable models the risk of non-normal histology (n = 27, borderline and rejection combined) rose with donor age (OR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01–1.10, p = 0.02) but not with the raw uptake ratio (OR 4.11, 95% CI 0.91–18.48, p = 0.07), though the standardised Z-score of that ratio did reach significance (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.02–2.33, p = 0.04). Crucially, the outcome that matters clinically — biopsy-proven subclinical rejection in its own right — showed no significant association with uptake at all. The authors' conclusion is blunt: the kidney-to-psoas uptake ratio does not reliably rule out subclinical rejection on surveillance biopsy. With only nine rejection events the study is underpowered to exclude a modest signal, but for UK units weighing whether to invest in PET-based surveillance the practical answer is that the biopsy stays, and non-invasive surveillance is better pursued through the molecular and cell-free DNA route.

### 5. [Crescents in native kidney biopsies from patients with IgA nephropathy and the risk of recurrence after kidney transplantation: a retrospective cohort study, systematic literature review and meta-analysis of observational studies](https://doi.org/10.1093/joneph/aajag169)
[Guzzo G, Al-Gobari M, Jaques C, Teta D, Pascual M, Herrera-Gomez F. *J Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42696417.]{.kw-ref}

Crescents in a native IgA nephropathy biopsy are a well-established marker of progression to kidney failure, and it has been a reasonable clinical intuition that the same aggressive phenotype would predict recurrence in the allograft — an intuition this combined cohort and meta-analysis tests and does not support. The authors first examined the 63 patients with IgA nephropathy transplanted at Lausanne University Hospital between 2003 and 2019 and found no association between glomerular crescents on the native biopsy and recurrence in the graft. They then searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science and PMC from inception to November 2025, excluding reviews, and identified five further cohorts, pooling aggregate data across 311 patients using the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment with heterogeneity quantified by I² and reporting bias inspected on a funnel plot. Recurrent IgA nephropathy affected 23% of the pooled population, and the prevalence of crescents in the contributing cohorts ranged widely from 12% to 62%. The pooled risk ratio for recurrence in patients with crescents was 1.53 (95% CI 0.40–5.90, p = 0.41) — a point estimate that looks worrying but with a confidence interval so wide that it is entirely compatible with both a halving and a near-sixfold increase in risk. The authors preserve the distinction that matters: crescents, particularly when affecting more than 25% of viable glomeruli, remain an unfavourable prognostic sign for progression of IgA nephropathy in the native kidney, but they may not be a risk factor for recurrence after transplantation. With 311 patients across six observational cohorts and that degree of imprecision this is better read as an absence of demonstrated association than as demonstrated safety, but for a UK surgeon counselling a young patient with crescentic IgA nephropathy about their transplant, it argues against treating the native histology as a reason for pessimism about the graft.

### 6. [The Precision and Accuracy of Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration Creatinine, Cystatin C, and Creatinine-Cystatin C Equations in Kidney Transplant Recipients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xkme.2026.101444)
[Mankan K, Wongyikul P, Khongthon N, Sripusanapan A, Noppakun K, Tantisattamo E, Danpanichkul P, Phinyo P, Chatatikun M, Phongphithakchai A. *Kidney Med*, 2026. PMID: 42668583.]{.kw-ref}

The 2024 KDIGO guidance endorses cystatin C for estimating glomerular filtration rate in chronic kidney disease but says comparatively little about transplant recipients, in whom steroid-related changes in muscle mass make the creatinine assumption particularly fragile — the gap this systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024506221) addresses. The authors sought peer-reviewed studies reporting CKD-EPI-based estimates against measured GFR in adult kidney transplant recipients, with two reviewers independently extracting study characteristics, GFR measurement method, equation type, mean bias and accuracy within 30% and 10% of measured GFR, resolving disagreement by consensus and pooling with random-effects models. Twenty-six studies met inclusion criteria and 14 provided extractable bias data, covering 4,041 adult recipients and 11,997 repeated measurements. The combined creatinine–cystatin C equation was the least biased, at 0.63 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI −3.65 to 4.92) — an interval straddling zero. The single-marker equations erred in opposite directions: creatinine-based estimates underestimated measured GFR by 4.95 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI −9.10 to −0.81), while cystatin C-based estimates overestimated it by 5.01 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 0.54 to 9.48), both intervals excluding zero. Accuracy within 30% and within 10% was broadly similar across the three biomarker approaches, so the advantage of the combined equation lies in bias rather than in precision, and the authors are candid that heterogeneity in reference GFR method, assay calibration and timing after transplantation limits what can be pooled. Their recommendation is measured — where cystatin C is available the combined equation is a reasonable choice, with multicentre validation under harmonised protocols still needed. For UK practice, where cystatin C availability varies considerably between laboratories, the useful takeaway is directional: a creatinine-only estimate in a transplant recipient is likely to read about 5 mL/min/1.73 m² low, which matters most at the thresholds where listing, drug dosing and graft survival counselling decisions are actually made.

### 7. [Effects of dapagliflozin on proteinuria, glycemic control, and treatment burden in diabetic kidney transplant recipients: a matched cohort study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00592-026-02792-4)
[Ural Z, Derici U. *Acta Diabetol*, 2026. PMID: 42675203.]{.kw-ref}

SGLT2 inhibitors have transformed cardiorenal risk management in chronic kidney disease, but transplant recipients were excluded from the pivotal trials and the evidence base for using them after transplantation remains thin — the gap this small retrospective study addresses. From a Turkish cohort of 282 transplant recipients followed between 2010 and 2022, 68 had diabetes; 18 started dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and formed the tolerability cohort, three stopped before three months for reasons of patient preference unrelated to documented adverse events, and the remaining 15 who completed at least 12 months were matched 1:1 on prespecified criteria against 15 diabetic recipients not taking an SGLT2 inhibitor. Proteinuria fell substantially more in the treated group, with a median change of −157 mg/day (IQR −310 to −52) against −12 mg/day (−48 to +25) in controls, a Hodges-Lehmann location shift of −171 mg/day (95% CI −310 to −32, p = 0.009), while graft function was unchanged (between-group difference in ΔeGFR +1.6 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI −1.8 to +5.0, p = 0.31). Glycaemic control improved more on treatment, HbA1c falling from 8.10% (65 mmol/mol) to 7.10% (54 mmol/mol) versus 8.18% (66 mmol/mol) to 7.80% (62 mmol/mol) in controls, with greater reductions also in fasting glucose and daily insulin dose. On safety there were two urinary tract infections needing oral antibiotics in the dapagliflozin group and one in controls, with no genital infections, ketoacidosis, acute rejection, graft loss, cardiovascular events, hospitalised infection or deaths recorded. Thirty patients in a retrospective, single-centre, completer-analysed cohort cannot establish either efficacy or safety, and the authors say so directly, calling for larger prospective multicentre studies before routine implementation. For UK units already fielding requests to continue or start SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetic recipients, this adds a modest reassuring data point on urinary and genital infection risk in a population where that is the main hesitation, without being anywhere near the evidence needed to justify a protocol change.

### 8. [Regional Disparities in Living Donor Kidney Transplantation: An Analysis of Transplant Referral Networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.08.020)
[McMichael LC, Cross N, Wyburn K, Clayton P, Wyld M. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42692200.]{.kw-ref}

Living donor transplantation is the preferred treatment for most patients with kidney failure, which makes geographical variation in who actually receives one a health system failure rather than a curiosity — the question this registry analysis quantifies at the level of the referral network rather than the individual centre. The authors included 53,313 adults who started kidney replacement therapy in Australia and New Zealand between 2002 and 2022, mapped each to a transplant referral network, and for each network compared the observed number of living donor transplants within 12 months against the number expected from multivariate Poisson regression with a random effect per network, yielding a standardised living donor transplant ratio. The spread was wide: ratios of observed to expected transplants ranged from 0.36 to 2.11 across the 21 networks, a near-sixfold difference between the lowest and highest, with four networks (19%) performing below expectation. Three factors were associated with higher rates of living donor transplantation — starting kidney replacement therapy at a centre directly affiliated with a transplant unit, non-metropolitan residence, and timely nephrology referral. The non-metropolitan finding is the counter-intuitive one, cutting against the usual assumption that distance from a transplant centre is the barrier, and the paper is an abstract-length report that does not decompose these associations further. The authors conclude that identifying the centre-level barriers and facilitators behind this variation is the necessary next step towards targeted strategies, which is a fair statement of what registry data of this kind can and cannot deliver: it locates the variation without explaining it. Australia and New Zealand differ from the UK in geography and in transplant service configuration, so the numbers do not transfer — but the method does, and the finding that affiliation between the dialysis unit and the transplant centre predicts living donation is a hypothesis worth testing against UK Renal Registry data, particularly alongside recent UK work on inequity in access after transplant failure.
